title: FOIA Program — Public Access to Agency Records
description: U.S. federal Freedom of Information Act program blueprint: one mission with the outcomes it seeks and ways to measure them, seven capabilities with their reference requirements, example implementation patterns with their tradeoffs, and discovery question sets for FOIA results and for request processing. It builds on Common Capabilities for case management, records, identity and access, and data protection.
jurisdictions: United States — federal agencies subject to the Freedom of Information Act

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 552 — Public information; agency rules, opinions, orders, records, and proceedings (Freedom of Information Act)
sources.note: What agencies must publish and post, the 20-working-day time limit and its extensions, expedited processing, appeals, the foreseeable harm standard, segregable release, tracking numbers, FOIA Public Liaisons, OGIS, the national request portal, and the contents of the annual FOIA report.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Justice — Guide to the Freedom of Information Act
sources.note: The Office of Information Policy’s treatise on the FOIA, with chapters on proactive disclosures, procedural requirements such as searches and response letters, fees and fee waivers, and each exemption.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Information Policy — Guidance on Backlog Reduction Plans
sources.note: Agencies should aim to keep their backlog below 10% of the requests they receive each year, and plan how to reduce it.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Justice — Handbook for Agency Annual FOIA Reports (2024 update)
sources.note: How agencies count what the annual FOIA report includes. A backlogged request is one still pending at the end of the fiscal year beyond the time the law allows for a response.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Information Policy — Guidelines for 2026 Chief FOIA Officer Reports
sources.note: What each agency’s Chief FOIA Officer reports each year, including proactive disclosures, use of technology, and managing backlogs and the oldest pending requests.

sources.title: National Archives — Office of Government Information Services (OGIS)
sources.note: The FOIA ombudsman: resolves disputes between requesters and agencies through mediation, and reviews agencies’ FOIA policies, procedures, and compliance.

sources.title: FOIA.gov — the government’s central website for FOIA
sources.note: Where the public can start a request with any agency, and where agencies’ annual and quarterly FOIA data is published.

sources.title: National Archives, Office of Government Information Services — Leveraging Technology to Improve FOIA Searches
sources.note: How agencies use technology, including e-discovery tools, to search for records, and the backlogs that can build when searches depend on IT offices.

sources.title: FOIA.gov — Developer resources
sources.note: The agency API for receiving requests submitted through the national FOIA portal.

sources.title: Section508.gov — IT accessibility for federal agencies
sources.note: Federal agencies’ information and communication technology, including web content and documents, must be accessible to people with disabilities.

sources.title: NIST — Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.note: A framework for voluntary use in managing the risks of AI systems, built around four functions, govern, map, measure, and manage, and the characteristics of trustworthy AI, such as being valid, accountable, and fair.

elements.title: FOIA Program
elements.description: Give the public access to agency records: post what the law requires without waiting to be asked, answer requests promptly, and release everything the law allows, withholding only what an exemption protects and release would foreseeably harm.

principles: Each request is one record from receipt to final response, with every letter and decision in it
The system keeps FOIA’s clock, with its tracks, working days, pauses, and extensions
Requests from FOIA.gov arrive as records, without retyping
Records are reviewed and redacted in one place, with each redaction marked with its exemption
Records people ask for again and again are posted without waiting for the next request
The annual report comes from the system of record, not from spreadsheets
AI suggests redactions, and staff decide

elements.title: Requests are answered within the time the law allows
elements.description: Requesters get a determination within 20 working days, or within the extension the law allows in unusual circumstances, and requests that qualify for expedited processing move faster.

measures.title: Time to process requests
measures.description: The median and average number of days to process simple, complex, and expedited requests, with the lowest and highest. Annual FOIA reports include these figures.

measures.title: Requests answered within 20 working days
measures.description: The share of processed requests answered within 20 working days. Annual FOIA reports group response times in 20-day bands.

elements.title: Overdue requests don’t pile up
elements.description: Few requests and appeals are still open past their legal deadline, and the oldest ones get closed.

measures.title: Backlogged requests
measures.description: Requests still pending at the end of the fiscal year beyond the time the law allows, compared with the number received that year. The Department of Justice suggests keeping it below 10% of requests received.

measures.title: Age of the oldest pending requests
measures.description: How long the agency’s ten oldest pending requests and ten oldest pending appeals have been open. Annual FOIA reports list them.

elements.title: Records are released unless the law calls for withholding
elements.description: Requesters get every record, and every reasonably segregable part of one, that the law allows. Information is withheld only under an exemption where release would foreseeably harm a protected interest, or where law prohibits release, and each withholding is marked.

measures.title: How requests are resolved
measures.description: The number of requests granted in full, granted in part, and denied, with how often each exemption was used. Annual FOIA reports include these figures.

elements.title: Records people often ask for are posted without a request
elements.description: The agency posts the records the law requires it to make available, including records released 3 or more times, so people can find them without filing a request.

measures.title: Records posted proactively
measures.description: The records made available online without a request, including frequently requested records. Annual FOIA reports count them, and Chief FOIA Officer reports describe them.

elements.title: Requesters can get help and resolve disputes
elements.description: Requesters can reach a FOIA Public Liaison with concerns, appeal an adverse determination, and turn to OGIS mediation instead of going to court.

measures.title: Time to decide appeals
measures.description: The median and average number of days to decide administrative appeals, against the 20 working days the law allows, and how the appeals came out. Annual FOIA reports include these figures.

elements.title: The program’s performance is open to view
elements.description: The Attorney General, OGIS, Congress, and the public can see how the agency’s FOIA program is doing through its annual, quarterly, and Chief FOIA Officer reports and their data.

measures.title: Annual FOIA report on time
measures.description: Whether the annual FOIA report reaches the Attorney General and OGIS by February 1, and is posted online with its raw data.

elements.title: Request Intake
elements.description: Ability to receive FOIA requests through the national portal and the agency’s own channels, log and acknowledge each one, work with requesters to make requests clear, and decide each request’s processing track, fee category, and whether it qualifies for expedited processing.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Each agency’s FOIA regulations set what makes a request proper, how its tracks and fee categories work, and who decides on expedited processing. Requests for records about the requester may also fall under the Privacy Act.

elements.title: Records Search & Collection
elements.description: Ability to find the records a request covers wherever the agency keeps them, including email and other electronic systems, collect them for review, and document how the search was done.
elements.applicabilityNotes: A search needs to be reasonably calculated to find the records asked for. What that takes depends on how and where the agency keeps its records.

elements.title: Review, Redaction & Consultation
elements.description: Ability to review the records found line by line, decide what can be released under the foreseeable harm standard, redact only what an exemption protects, and consult or refer other agencies with an interest in the records.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Exemptions, exclusions, and consultation practices are technical. This describes the ability, not how to apply any exemption.

elements.title: Response & Release
elements.description: Ability to send each requester a determination that explains what was released and withheld and why, with their appeal rights and where to get help, and to deliver released records in the form asked for.

elements.title: Appeals & Requester Assistance
elements.description: Ability to help requesters through a FOIA Public Liaison, decide administrative appeals of adverse determinations, and work with OGIS when a requester seeks mediation.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Who decides appeals, and how the FOIA Public Liaison works with requesters, is set by each agency.

elements.title: Proactive Disclosure
elements.description: Ability to publish the records the law requires agencies to make available without a request, such as final opinions, policy statements, staff manuals, and records released 3 or more times, in an online FOIA library people can search.

elements.title: FOIA Reporting
elements.description: Ability to compile the annual FOIA report, quarterly reports, and the Chief FOIA Officer report from the agency’s request data, and post them and their raw data online.

elements.title: Accept requests from the national portal
elements.description: Take in requests submitted through FOIA.gov alongside the agency’s own channels, without retyping them.

elements.title: Place each request on a processing track
elements.description: Decide whether a request is simple, complex, or expedited, and decide on expedited processing within 10 calendar days of the request.

elements.title: Work with requesters to clarify requests
elements.description: Contact requesters to clarify or narrow what they’re asking for, record what was agreed, and offer a faster track when narrowing would allow one.

elements.title: Set fees and decide fee waivers
elements.description: Place each requester in a fee category, estimate fees, decide fee waiver requests, and charge no search fees when the agency misses a deadline without an allowed exception.

elements.title: Search every place records are kept
elements.description: Search the systems, email, shared drives, and paper files likely to hold the records asked for, by terms, dates, and the people who hold them.

elements.title: Document each search
elements.description: Record where the agency searched, the terms and dates used, and who searched, so the search can be shown to be adequate.

elements.title: Set duplicates aside before review
elements.description: Find exact and near duplicates, such as copies of the same email thread, so each record is reviewed once.

elements.title: Mark each redaction with its exemption
elements.description: Show on the released record where information was withheld, how much, and under which exemption, unless showing it would reveal what the exemption protects.

elements.title: Release every segregable part
elements.description: Release the parts of a record that can reasonably be separated from what’s exempt, instead of withholding whole pages.

elements.title: Record why each withholding is needed
elements.description: Record the exemption and the foreseeable harm behind each withholding, so the decision can be explained on appeal or in court.

elements.title: Consult and refer other agencies
elements.description: Send records another agency has an interest in for consultation or referral, follow them until they come back, and tell the requester when part of a request was referred.

elements.title: Protect records before redaction
elements.description: Limit who can see records before they’re redacted to the people processing the request, and keep a record of access.

elements.title: Send complete determination letters
elements.description: Tell the requester what was found, released, and withheld and why. For an adverse determination, include the right to appeal within at least 90 days and to seek help from the FOIA Public Liaison and OGIS.

elements.title: Deliver records in the format asked for
elements.description: Provide records in the form or format the requester asks for when they can readily be reproduced that way, such as electronic files.

elements.title: Release large requests in parts
elements.description: Release records as they’re ready, in interim releases, when a request is large enough that waiting for all of it would delay everything.

elements.title: Decide appeals within 20 working days
elements.description: Log each administrative appeal, review the original determination independently, and decide it within 20 working days.

elements.title: Answer questions about where a request stands
elements.description: Let requesters find out the status of a request, including an estimated date of completion, by phone or online, and reach a FOIA Public Liaison with concerns.

elements.title: Work with OGIS on mediation
elements.description: Respond when OGIS contacts the agency about a dispute, and keep track of mediation cases and their results.

elements.title: Spot records requested 3 or more times
elements.description: Notice when the same records have been requested 3 or more times, and post them once they’re released.

elements.title: Keep an online FOIA library
elements.description: Post the records the law requires in an online library people can search, in accessible formats.

elements.title: Compile the annual FOIA report on time
elements.description: Gather the statistics the law requires for the fiscal year, such as requests received and processed, how they were resolved, exemptions used, processing times, backlog, and fees, and submit them by February 1.

elements.title: Post the reports and their raw data
elements.description: Make each report and the raw statistics behind it available online.

elements.title: FOIA Request Processing
elements.description: An example architecture: one place to handle a FOIA request from start to finish. It takes requests from the national portal and the agency’s own form, tracks them on FOIA’s tracks and deadlines, collects records and sets duplicates aside, applies marked redactions, publishes releases to the FOIA library, and produces the annual report from the same data.

parts: Request intake from the national portal and the agency’s own form
Request tracking with FOIA’s tracks, working-day deadlines, fee categories, and correspondence
A review workspace that collects records, sets duplicates aside, and applies redactions marked with their exemptions
Release packages and determination letters from templates
Publishing to the online FOIA library
Annual and quarterly report figures from the request data
strengths: The annual report’s figures come from the same records staff work in
The requester’s whole history is in one place
fitsWhen: Tracking and review happen in separate tools today, with retyping between them
watchFor: Moving open requests from an old system mid-year can disturb the annual report’s counts
A hosted system needs a security authorization before it can hold unredacted records

ways.title: A FOIA product
ways.description: A product made for FOIA that handles tracking, review, release, and reporting in one place.
strengths: Knows FOIA’s rules, such as tracks, working-day deadlines, fee categories, and exemption codes
fitsWhen: The office handles hundreds of requests a year or more
watchFor: Built-in review may struggle with very large email collections

ways.title: The shared case platform, with a separate review tool
ways.description: Requests tracked on the agency’s shared case platform, set up for FOIA’s tracks and deadlines, with a separate document review tool for collecting, deduplicating, and redacting records, and a handoff between the two.
strengths: Uses a platform the agency already has for the tracking
Either tool can be replaced without replacing the other
Suits offices that already own a review tool
fitsWhen: The agency’s shared case platform is well supported
Request volume is moderate, and records are mostly documents rather than large email collections
watchFor: The handoff between the tools is where requests stall or records go missing
Deadline rules, such as pausing the clock, must be built and kept up to date
Two tools to authorize, secure, and train people on

elements.title: Request Tracking with a Separate Review Tool
elements.description: An example architecture: requests tracked on the agency’s shared case platform, set up for FOIA’s tracks and deadlines, with a separate document review tool for collecting, deduplicating, and redacting records, and a handoff between the two.

parts: FOIA request tracking set up on the agency’s shared case platform
A deadline calculator for working days, extensions, and pauses for clarification or fees
A document review and redaction tool that marks exemptions
A link from each request to its set of records in review, and the release package back
Annual report figures from the tracking data
strengths: Uses a platform the agency already has for the tracking
Either tool can be replaced without replacing the other
Suits offices that already own a review tool
fitsWhen: The agency’s shared case platform is well supported
Request volume is moderate, and records are mostly documents rather than large email collections
watchFor: The handoff between the tools is where requests stall or records go missing
Deadline rules, such as pausing the clock, must be built and kept up to date
Two tools to authorize, secure, and train people on

ways.title: The shared case platform, with a separate review tool

elements.title: Email Search with eDiscovery Tools
elements.description: An example architecture: the agency’s eDiscovery tools search mailboxes and other collections by people, terms, and dates, set aside duplicates and thread email conversations, and send what’s found to review, with each search recorded.

parts: Searches across mailboxes, chats, and shared files by person, terms, and date range
Deduplication and email threading before review
A record of each search’s terms, sources, and results
Export of the results to the review tool, or review in place
Coordination with the IT staff who run the searches
strengths: Handles large email collections far better than typical FOIA software
The search record helps show that the search was adequate
Reviewers see each conversation once
fitsWhen: The agency already licenses eDiscovery tools for litigation or investigations
watchFor: Searches can wait in IT’s queue for a long time
For a single known record, asking the person who keeps it is faster
Threading and deduplication need checking, since copies still slip through

elements.title: Requests from the National Portal by API
elements.description: An example architecture: the agency’s FOIA system receives requests submitted on FOIA.gov through the portal’s agency API, so each one arrives as a request record with its fields filled in, instead of as an email to retype.

parts: A connection in the agency’s FOIA system that implements the portal’s agency API
A mapping from the portal’s fields to the agency’s request record
An acknowledgment with the tracking number sent back to the requester
Monitoring for requests that fail to arrive
The agency’s FOIA.gov contact and component details kept current
strengths: No retyping, so fewer errors and faster logging
Requests reach the right component directly
One intake path for portal requests and the agency’s own form
fitsWhen: The agency has an automated FOIA case system
Portal requests arrive by email today
watchFor: Changes to the portal’s API need following
Each component’s routing must match how FOIA.gov lists it

ways.title: A connection to FOIA.gov’s agency API

elements.title: FOIA Library Publishing
elements.description: An example architecture: released records go from the review tool to the agency’s online FOIA library with a title, date, and request number, in accessible formats, and records requested 3 or more times are flagged for posting.

parts: A FOIA library section of the agency’s website, with search
A publishing step from the review tool that carries each release’s details
A check that released files are accessible, such as text-searchable PDFs
A list of records requested 3 or more times, from the tracking data
A hold on records released to people about themselves, which aren’t for public posting
strengths: Posting becomes part of closing a request
Repeat requests can be answered with a link
fitsWhen: Releases are posted by hand, if at all
Several requesters ask for the same records
watchFor: Records released to people about themselves must never be posted
Making older scanned records accessible takes effort
Posted records still follow a records schedule

elements.title: AI Suggestions in Records Review
elements.description: An example architecture: the review tool suggests passages that may fall under an exemption, groups near-duplicate records, and flags personal information, and the reviewer decides every redaction and records the exemption that applies.

parts: Suggested redactions for patterns such as Social Security numbers, phone numbers, and names
Passages that may fall under an exemption, each with the reason it was suggested
Groups of near-duplicate records and email threads, so one decision applies consistently
The reviewer’s decision on every suggestion, with the exemption recorded
Checks of how often suggestions are accepted, by kind
strengths: Reviewers spend less time finding routine personal information
Similar records get the same treatment
Large releases move faster without lowering the bar for what’s withheld
fitsWhen: The office reviews large volumes of email and documents
Its review tool offers these features, or can add them
watchFor: Exemptions turn on judgment, including the foreseeable harm standard, so a person decides every withholding
Relying on suggestions can lead to withholding more than the law allows
Records under review hold sensitive information, so the model must run where the records are allowed to be

elements.title: FOIA Workload Dashboard from Tracking Data
elements.description: An example architecture: a dashboard built on the request tracking data that shows the backlog, the oldest open requests, time to respond on each track, and work by team, refreshed daily, so leaders can act long before the annual report.

parts: A daily copy of the tracking data in a reporting store
Measures defined the way the annual report counts them, such as backlogged requests
Views of the backlog, the oldest requests, and response times by track and team
Forecasts of incoming requests from past volumes, for planning staff
Access for the Chief FOIA Officer, managers, and staff
strengths: Leaders see the backlog as it grows, not once a year
Counts match the annual report, so there are no surprises when it’s due
Changes to staffing and process can be checked against results
fitsWhen: The tracking system’s data can be copied out every day
Leaders want to act on the goal of keeping the backlog under 10% during the year
watchFor: Definitions must match the handbook, or the dashboard and the report will disagree
Request details can be sensitive, so dashboards should show counts rather than requesters
